passages.happening:
‘When Mordecai learned of all that had happened, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the middle of the city, wailing loudly and bitterly’ (verse 1). He goes only as far as the king's gate, because no one in sackcloth may go through it.

‘In every province to which the king’s command and edict came, there was great mourning among the Jews. They fasted, wept, and lamented, and many lay in sackcloth and ashes’ (verse 3).

Esther hears that Mordecai is in mourning and is overcome with distress. She sends him clothes, but he will not take them. So she sends Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs assigned to her, to find out what is wrong. Mordecai tells him everything, even the exact sum Haman had promised to the treasury, and gives him a copy of the decree to show Esther, ‘urging her to approach the king, implore his favor, and plead before him for her people’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Tearing clothes and wearing sackcloth and ashes were the ordinary signs of grief and shame in Israel and among its neighbors. Sackcloth was a coarse cloth, often of goat hair, and ashes on the head showed a person brought low. Fasting went with mourning and with urgent prayer.

Signs of mourning were kept out of the king's presence, where everything was meant to be joy, so Mordecai cannot pass the gate.

Esther cannot simply go out to meet him. She lives in the women's quarters of the palace, and messages pass through eunuchs. Hathach becomes the go-between on whom a people's survival hangs. And the chapter is built as an exchange of messages, each round raising the stakes.
passages.later: Mourning like this fills the prophets and the psalms. Daniel, in exile, turned to God ‘with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes’ (Daniel 9:3).
passages.hard:
The decree has gone out, and a whole people is in mourning. The book does not hurry past their grief. It names the fasting, the weeping and the sackcloth in every province, and it lets Mordecai wail aloud in the middle of the city.

Grief like this is not a lack of faith. In the Bible it is often how faith speaks when everything is at stake.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Mordecai would not put on the clothes Esther sent until something was done. Ask whether you have ever tried to comfort someone's grief without dealing with its cause. And ask whose mourning you need to hear before you try to cover it.

passages.t: For such a time as this
passages.happening:
Esther sends word back. Everyone knows the law: anyone who goes to the king in the inner court without being called is put to death, unless the king holds out his gold scepter. “But I have not been summoned to appear before the king for the past thirty days” (verse 11).

Mordecai answers: “Do not imagine that because you are in the king’s palace you alone will escape the fate of all the Jews” (verse 13). “For if you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place, but you and your father’s house will perish. And who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (verse 14).

Esther decides. “Go and assemble all the Jews who can be found in Susa, and fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day, and I and my maidens will fast as you do. After that, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish!” (verse 16).

‘So Mordecai went and did all that Esther had instructed him’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
This is the hinge of the book. Until now Esther has been taken and moved by others. Here she decides and gives the orders, and the chapter ends with Mordecai doing what she told him.

The rule Esther describes fits what Greek writers say about the seclusion of the Persian kings, who were approached only through officials and ceremony. Reliefs from the palace at Persepolis show the king on his throne holding a long scepter as an official is brought before him. That Esther had not been called for thirty days suggests that her standing with an unpredictable king was uncertain, which makes the risk real.

Mordecai's reply is the book's clearest statement of its outlook, and it never names God. Deliverance will come from another place. The word is found only here in the Old Testament. Mordecai is sure that rescue will come; what is uncertain is whether Esther will be part of it. And time here means a fitting moment, a moment for action.

A fast of three days without food or water is severe. In the Old Testament fasting nearly always goes with prayer, so a first reader would assume that the Jews of Susa were praying, though the book does not say so. Many Jewish communities later kept a fast before Purim, the Fast of Esther, remembering this chapter.
passages.later: Jacob, sending his youngest son to Egypt, spoke in the same way: ‘As for me, if I am bereaved, I am bereaved’ (Genesis 43:14). And when Paul faced his accusers, he said, ‘I do not refuse to die’ (Acts 25:11), with something of Esther's courage.
passages.hard:
Why doesn't the book's turning point mention God or prayer at all?

Esther is one of only two books of the Hebrew Bible, with the Song of Songs, that never mention God, and its silence is most striking here. Mordecai speaks of relief from another place, and Esther calls a fast without a word about prayer.

Readers explain this in several ways. Many see the silence as deliberate: the book shows God working hiddenly, through ordinary choices and apparent coincidences, as he often seems to work in a world where he is not seen. Some suggest that a book meant to be read at a noisy festival, or written for Jews living under a foreign empire, spoke of God with reserve. Some take another place as a reverent way of pointing to God without naming him; others read it as meaning only another human source of help.

The Greek translation of Esther adds long prayers by Mordecai and Esther and names God often, which shows that ancient readers felt the silence too. The Hebrew text leaves the reader to see the hand that the characters do not name.
passages.asks: Mordecai asked whether Esther had been put where she was for this very moment. Ask where you have been placed, and for whom you could speak there. And ask what it would cost you to stop keeping quiet.
